In [[mathematics]], a '''Hopfian group''' is a [[group (mathematics)|group]] ''G'' for which every [[surjective function|surjective ]][[group homomorphism|homomorphism]] ''G'' → ''G'' is an [[isomorphism]]. Equivalently, a group is Hopfian if and only if it is not isomorphic to any of its proper [[quotient group|quotient]]s.{{sfnp|Bouyer|2013|loc=definition 7.6}}

A group ''G'' is [[co-Hopfian group|co-Hopfian]] if every [[injective function|injective]] homomorphism ''G'' → ''G'' is an isomorphism.  Equivalently, ''G'' is not isomorphic to any of its proper [[subgroup]]s.

Hopfian groups are named after [[Heinz Hopf]].

==Examples of Hopfian groups==
* Every [[finite group]], by an elementary counting argument. 
* More generally, every [[polycyclic-by-finite group]].
* Any [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]] [[free group]].
* The additive group <math>\Q</math> of [[rational number|rationals]].
* Any [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]] [[residually finite group]].
* Any [[word-hyperbolic group]].

==Examples of non-Hopfian groups==
* [[Quasicyclic group]]s.
* The additive group <math>\R</math> of [[real number]]s.{{sfnp|Clark|2012|loc="This is because ('''R''',+) is torsion-free and divisible and thus a '''Q'''-vector space. So -- since every vector space has a basis, by the Axiom of Choice -- it is isomorphic to the direct sum of copies of ('''Q''',+) indexed by a set of continuum cardinality. This makes the Hopfian property clear"}}
* The [[Baumslag–Solitar group]] <math>B(2,3)</math>. In general <math>B(m,n)</math> is non-Hopfian if and only if there exists primes <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> with <math>p\mid m</math>, <math>q\mid n</math> and <math>p\nmid n</math>, <math>q\nmid m</math>.{{sfnp|Bouyer|2013|loc=theorem 7.7}}

==Properties==

It was shown by Collins that it is an [[undecidable problem]] to determine, given a [[Presentation_of_a_group#finitely_presented|finite presentation]] of a group, whether the group is Hopfian.{{sfnp|Collins|1969}} Unlike the undecidability of many properties of groups, this is not a consequence of the [[Adian–Rabin theorem]] because Hopficity is not a [[Adian–Rabin theorem#Markov property|Markov property]].{{sfnp|Miller|Schupp|1971}}
